title: Caruana Hits 2800, Within 7.2 Points Of Carlsen's World No. 1 Spot
summary:
GM Fabiano Caruana is now rated exactly 2800.0 on the live rating list after beating GM Vincent Keymer, while GM Magnus Carlsen is just 7.2 rating points from losing his 15-year unbroken streak as world number-one after losing to GM Haik Martirosyan. The Armenian is the surprise leader of Group C of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026, while Caruana leads Group B. GM Alireza Firouzja leads Group A despite mixing up colors and losing his first game to GM Andrew Hong, while GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave has now defeated three Group D rivals in a row after overcoming GM Hans Niemann.

Day five, which features rounds seven and eight of the Group Stage, is on Saturday, November 14, starting at 9 a.m. ET / 15:00 CET / 7:30 p.m. IST.

Group A: Firouzja Bounces Back To Lead

Group B: Caruana Dominates But Le Keeps Up Pressure

Group C: Martirosyan Stuns Carlsen To Lead; Giri A Point Behind

Group D: MVL Tops Table With 3rd Match Win In A Row

Group Stage Round 5 Results

There were some huge upsets in round five, as half the games ended decisively.

The evening round was quieter, but featured some significant wins.

Group Stage Round 6 Results

Group A: Firouzja Bounces Back To Lead

Firouzja's first loss had few consequences since he struck back immediately to beat Hong. His three-point haul for the day took him a point further ahead of his pursuers GMs Jan-Krzysztof Duda and Levon Aronian, who drew against each other. GM Jorden van Foreest was the player to climb, inflicting yet another loss on the suffering GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov.

Group A Standings

Firouzja revealed he had an unpleasant surprise in the first game of the day, having made a mistake Keymer confessed to making the day before:

I didn’t know I’ll play the first game Black—I thought I always have White in the group, so I didn’t prepare anything with Black, so this was the shock. And then I didn’t play well in the first game.

Firouzja was surprised to find he had the black pieces in the first game vs. Hong. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

In a sharp Sicilian, Firouzja found his king incredibly exposed, but he did have the clock on his side, with 19 minutes to just more than one as things became critical. He chose the wrong side of the board to try and hide, however, and then 27...Qf7? was the last nail in his coffin. Hong could have won with a dramatic rook sacrifice, but 28.Bb6! also got the job done just fine.

Firouzja struck back smoothly in the second game, however, with Hong admitting he wasn't sure exactly where he'd gone wrong.

Former World Rapid Champion Nodirbek Abdusattorov's shocking tournament continued against Jorden van Foreest. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

It was clear where Abdusattorov went astray against Van Foreest, with 21...Nxc4? only worsening an already tricky position.

Abdusattorov had chances in the second game, but they came to nothing.

Aronian and Duda canceled each other out. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Duda and Aronian played out two lively draws, with Aronian crediting his second GM Mikhail Antipov ("a great expert in this line") for the decision to play the rare 4...Ne7!? in the Anti-Berlin. It sent Duda into a 17-minute think.

Aronian called it "not entirely correct," but felt it could work in a "fast classic" game. It did, though in the end no blood was spilled. On that topic, Aronian had responded earlier in the day to the news that classical 45+30 games could now become widespread by suggesting a change in the K factor.

@FIDE_chess @ChrisBirdIA I feel that anything below 1 hour 30 minutes per game should have K=5 or K=6 factor. Somehow it doesn’t feel right to equate a 5-6 hour game to a 2.5 hour game.

— Levon Aronian (@LevAronian) November 13, 2026

The lower factor would mean that the games played in Budapest would affect ratings less, with equally-rated opponents earning three points for a win instead of five. That brings us to some dramatic shifts in the rating list.

Group B: Caruana Dominates, But Le Keeps Up Pressure

Caruana remains the top-performing player in the Total Chess Pilot, as he started day four with a fourth win in five games, this time against Keymer. Only GM Liem Le is relatively close after surviving two hair-raising games against GM Richard Rapport.

Group B Standings

Caruana's win, then draw, saw him gain 17 rating points, while Carlsen has now dropped 15.8, making it a remarkable 32.8-point swing in just three days of chess.

Carlsen started the tournament with a 40-point lead over Caruana.

Caruana's third win in a row against an elite rival saw him flawlessly convert a single easy-to-miss slip by Keymer. That's our Game of the Day, which GM Rafael Leitao has analyzed below.

"My play is flowing very well, I’m just playing quite confidently," said Caruana. He crossed 2800, but when asked if he was thinking about ratings and catching Carlsen, he responded: "No, not too much, I have reached 2800 a few times before. If it gets a bit closer, I’ll definitely think about it, but for the moment I’m not thinking about it too much."

Fabiano Caruana has spent six years as world number-two. Can he now take the number-one spot? Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

It was already perhaps closer than he realized, since Caruana could potentially have become world number-one during the second round of the day. As it happened, however, he admitted he'd been "very close to losing" in a 72-move rematch against Keymer.

Elsewhere in the group, all games were drawn, with GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu calling his first game against GM Vladislav Artemiev "crazy." In mutual time trouble, Artemiev had some chances, but he admitted overall he was happy to survive after Praggnanandhaa tried to exploit an extra pawn until move 89. A fast draw in the second game suited both players.

Artemiev was happy to end with two draws against Pragg, a player he described as "young and very dangerous." Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

In the remaining clash, Le admitted he was "quite lucky to survive both" games against Rapport. In the first, he blundered a simple tactic, while in the second, Rapport came to the confessional to express his surprise.

Rapport on 9...a6 vs. Le: "The funny thing is I have played this vs. Ding in 2017... now it's the engine's top choice, so I'm surprised he's thinking. The question is do I remember anything else after a6 & if I've checked that game... and the answer is no!" 😀 #TotalChess https://t.co/pXySG4jGO2

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 13, 2026

Rapport took over and gained a real advantage, but it fizzled out until he liquidated to a position where he was playing with two rooks against Le's queen. There were chances, but no breakthrough, until a draw was reached on move 103 in the last game of the day to finish. Perhaps unsurprisingly, Rapport didn't want to be interviewed after it was over.

Group C: Martirosyan Stuns Carlsen To Lead; Giri A Point Behind

Martirosyan's healthy habit of winning a game a day continued against none other than Carlsen, so that the Armenian star leads Group C while Carlsen languishes at the bottom of the table. The gap isn't insurmountable, but GM Anish Giri's win over GM Ian Nepomniachtchi puts him in a strong position. GMs Shakhriyar Mamedyarov and Abhimanyu Mishra made two draws.

Group C Standings

It's impossible not to wonder each day when Carlsen will "wake up," but, as his tournament and rating situation worsens, the pressure is only growing. Winless so far, he was almost forced to play for a win against 2669-rated Martirosyan, but the Armenian star is no pushover. In fact, Carlsen could also recall an earlier calamity against the same opponent, when he sent pieces flying and was adjudged to have lost in the 2025 World Blitz Championship.

Magnus sends the pieces scattering and desperately tries to set them up again, but to avoid losing on time like the day before he hits the clock with 2 seconds to spare without having finished the repairs! https://t.co/XcvkNAnMKI

— chess24 (@chess24com) December 30, 2025

In Budapest, time was again a factor, with Carlsen once more burning up too much time in the opening for very little reward. Although the world number-one managed to equalize on the board, it was a more pleasant position to play as White, with Martirosyan commenting: "When he had time trouble, I already felt like his king was weak and my king was safer, so I felt it’s very good chances to try to play for a win, and yeah—it worked well!"

If not for the 11-minute time difference, Black would be doing fine.

Martirosyan managed to weave a mating net around his opponent's king.

Martirosyan beats the world number-one. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Martirosyan commented: "It’s like a dream for me! I was just dreaming to play against him a classical game, but to win is already special. I will think about this moment many times."

It's like a dream for me!

—Haik Martirosyan on beating Magnus Carlsen

That loss after five draws was a heavy blow for Carlsen, but there was almost no time to recover, since half an hour later the next games would begin.

"Magnus, you're ready for a second game?" "No." #TotalChess https://t.co/4tEQdpUxNW

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 13, 2026

Carlsen is famous for his comebacks after losses, but his attempt to unsettle Martirosyan in the next game with 8.g4!?, played after a seven-minute think, looked a lot like tilt.

Martirosyan responded well, and once again it felt like all Carlsen's ingenuity was going into trying to extricate himself from a difficult situation on the board and clock of his own making. This time he managed, however, with a relieved Carlsen in good spirits afterward.

Relief and a smile for Magnus Carlsen as another risky adventure this time ends in a draw that keeps him as the World no. 1! #TotalChess https://t.co/n2lb7g5tP5

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 13, 2026

Still, while needing to win at all costs for the Total Chess standings, he also finds himself in the most rating danger he's been since the period around the 2018 World Championship match against Caruana, when the gap closed to three points.

That became a blip in over 15 years unbroken as world number-one, but suddenly the top spot is up for grabs again—while Carlsen is also in danger of falling below 2800 for the first time in 17 years.

Caruana was three points behind Carlsen when they played a world championship match. Now it's 7.2 points—a gap that could disappear in half a day. Image: Live Chess Rating.

As you can see, Giri is one player to have increased his rating, and he did it with a draw and win against GM Ian Nepomniachtchi on day four. In the first game, Nepomniachtchi unleashed a piece sacrifice and ended the game with more time than he began, but Giri defended well.

Nepomniachtchi wasn't thrilled with what he did to his position in the second game against Giri. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

In the second, both players identified it as carelessness from Nepomniachtchi that he got into trouble in what should have been a dead-drawn endgame.

Group D: MVL Tops Table With 3rd Match Win In A Row

Vachier-Lagrave is the only unbeaten player in Group D after scoring a win over Niemann to pull three points clear of the U.S. star, while GM Arjun Erigaisi is also three points back after winning what for GM Wesley So was another gut-wrenching game. GM Bibisara Assaubayeva is still very much in the hunt, but lost the second game after overcoming GM Vaishali Rameshbabu in the first.

Group D Standings

"I’m definitely playing well!" said Vachier-Lagrave, who after a comfortable draw in the first game beat Niemann with a sharp attack in the second—an opportunity he put down to "some very good prep thanks to my seconds who did some great work."

Vachier-Lagrave won the battle of two players who had been unbeaten up to this point. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

title: Teenage Phenom Wins Freestyle Friday
summary:
IM Khuong Duy Dau, the 15-year-old international master from Vietnam, won Freestyle Friday on November 13. A regular of both Freestyle Friday and Titled Tuesday, the win was Dau's first in either event, and he did it by 1.5 points ahead of second place. While Dau remains outside the top eight in the standings for the Freestyle Friday Championship (FFC), he made a significant move up from 14 points to 24.

2 | GM | Pranav V | 65 | Qualified from Split 1

4 | GM | Sina Movahed | 48 | In a qualifying position

8 | GM | Ian Nepomniachtchi | 30 | In a qualifying position

Zachary Saine, "TheChessNerd," commentated for Freestyle Chess, which you can view below:

For the first half of the tournament, it appeared GM Volodar Murzin, or perhaps GM Gata Kamsky, was likely to win. They were the only players to begin 4/4. When they faced in the fifth round, Kamsky got White and Murzin was lucky to escape with a draw, as IM Sahib Singh and GM Nguyen Ngoc Truong Son caught up with both of them.

Both Murzin and Kamsky won their next game to return to the shared lead among themselves, as White won on the first five boards. Both games were instant classics, with Murzin executing an almost perfect attack and Kamsky playing some star moves himself.

In the next round, Murzin got his first separation from Kamsky, defeating GM Parham Maghsoodloo, while GM Jeffery Xiong drew with Kamsky. It was here that Dau, who made two draws in the first five rounds, joined Kamsky in second, defeating IM Renato Terry.

Taking Black against Dau in round eight, Murzin had his first bad game of the tournament, which was enough for Dau to take the tournament lead, as Kamsky lost to GM Sevian. Dau's cheeky castling move was too much for Murzin to recover from, although he fought on for nearly 50 more moves.

Coming out of the ensuing break, Dau's rise and Murzin's fall both continued; Dau won with Black against GM Sam Sevian while Murzin lost with White to Xiong. With a draw in Kamsky vs. Maghsoodloo, Dau on eight points and Xiong on 7.5 were a full point or more ahead of everyone else.

Dau and Xiong had drawn each other in round five, so in round 10 they instead faced Maghsoodloo and last week's victor, GM Nodirbek Yakubboev, respectively. Maghsoodloo with White seemed to be pushing Dau to the limit when he suddenly blundered a piece, on what Saine suspected might be a mouse slip. Dau never let go in a 21-move rout.

But Xiong kept pace against Yakubboev, after Yakubboev missed his one chance at turning the tables after each player missed a tactical finesse.

With one round left, no one had locked up their tournament standing, but Dau had secured a top-two finish and was in control. He faced GM Oleksandr Bortnyk, who was looking for a miracle bounce-back from an 0/2 start, with Xiong taking on Nguyen while Murzin faced WFM Veronika Shubenkova with a chance at third. Murzin won in the first game to finish, but Nguyen was close behind, delivering the tournament to Dau.

For good measure, Dau won as well, becoming the first player to reach 10 points in Freestyle Friday since the tournament resumed in early October. Murzin ended up finishing second ahead of Xiong on the tournament tiebreak system, with Nguyen taking fourth place. Terry, Kamsky, and Bortnyk did not win cash with a top-four finish, but they did gain FFC points with a top-10 finish. Despite her final-round setback, Shubenkova had done enough to claim the women's prize.

title: Andreikin Nearly Sweeps 3 0 Thursday Tournaments
summary:
GM Dmitry Andreikin nearly scored a perfect sweep in the three 3 0 Thursday tournaments on November 12. No one has ever won more than two Thursday tournaments in the same week, but Andreikin came within half a point of a hat trick. He won the first two events, while taking second place, just behind GM Jeffery Xiong in the third tournament. Andreikin, who will compete next week against GM Denis Lazavik in the first round of the Speed Chess Championship, showed that he is in top form.

First Tournament: Andreikin Catches Oro

In the first tournament of the day, the youngest GM in the world, 13-year-old Faustino Oro, nearly won his first 3 0 Thursday. He won his first five games and held a sixth-round draw against the highest-rated player in the field, GM Hikaru Nakamura. He maintained the lead, heading into the final round with 8.5 points, ahead of Andreikin on tiebreaks.

Andreikin kept pace with Oro by defeating GM Parham Maghsoodloo in the 10th round. It was Maghsoodloo's only blemish in the event. He started after the first round and then scored 9/10 to tie for second place!

That game set up a final-round battle between Oro and Andreikin to decide first place. Oro dealt with a dangerous attack and survived to an equal endgame, but missed a fork, allowing Andreikin to win the tournament.

The victory gave Andreikin 9.5 points, the highest score of any player throughout the day. GM Christopher Yoo had the best tiebreaks among players on nine points, placing him in second, while Xiong took third, and Maghsoodloo finished fourth. FM Iren Lyutsinger won the women's prize with seven points.

The top 10 finishers in the first tournament.

Second Tournament: Andreikin Repeats

Andreikin didn't let a fourth-round loss against GM Maksim Chigaev slow him down in the second tournament. He won in the next round to reach 4/5 and then had another game with the black pieces against Maghsoodloo.

After a seventh-round draw with IM Reza Mahdavi, Andreikin faced GM Sergei Zhigalko. In a complicated tactical battle, Andreikin emerged with another win.

Andreikin finished well to end on nine points, a half-point ahead of Maghsoodloo and IM Renato Terry, who took second and third place respectively. GM Alexandra Kosteniuk won the women's prize with seven points.

The top 10 finishers in the second tournament.

Third Tournament: Xiong Narrowly Prevents Andreikin Sweep

Andreikin had a slow start to the third tournament, dropping his second-round game against FM S Bijoy Arpith. However, he bounced back by winning his next four games, including a sharp battle against Xiong in the sixth round.

At that point it seemed like Andreikin might win every tournament. However, Xiong went on to take his next three games, including this attacking effort against GM Jules Moussard in the seventh round.

Meanwhile, Andreikin lost in the seventh round to FM Hamidreza Tahmasebi and only managed a draw against Maghsoodloo in the ninth round (their third game of the day). Andreikin finished with 8.5 points and strong tiebreaks. It wasn't quite enough as Xiong drew his final two games to end on nine points to reach first place. Tahmasebi took third with eight points, while IM Rose Atwell won the women's prize with 6.5 points.

The top 10 finishers in the third tournament.

3 0 Thursday is a set of three weekly Swiss tournaments for verified titled players featuring their favorite time control. Each of the three tournaments is an 11-round Swiss with a 3+0 time control. The combined prize fund is $3,000 every week.

title: Martirosyan defeats Carlsen on Day 3 in Budapest
summary: Caruana extends his lead, and Vachier-Lagrave moves into clear first Haik Martirosyan defeated Magnus Carlsen and took the outright lead in Group C on the third day of the Fast Classic group stage at the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest. Andrew Hong also caused an upset by handing Group A leader Alireza Firouzja his first defeat of the group stage. Games 5 and 6 produced 10 decisive results from 24 encounters. Each player again faced the same opponent twice with colours reversed, with three points awarded for a win and one for a draw. After six games per player, all four groups have outright leaders. Firouzja heads Group A on eleven points, Fabiano Caruana leads Group B on fourteen, Martirosyan tops Group C on ten, and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave leads Group D on twelve. Firouzja strikes back after Hong claims his first win Andrew Hong recorded his first Fast Classic victory of the event by defeating Alireza Firouzja with White in a complicated battle. Firouzja responded with a White win in the return game, creating an advantage and forcing favourable exchanges before securing the win. The three points apiece leave Firouzja on eleven and Hong on six. Jan-Krzysztof Duda and Levon Aronian drew both games. Duda remains second on nine points, two behind Firouzja, with Aronian on seven. Jorden van Foreest collected four points against Nodirbek Abdusattorov, winning their first encounter before drawing the return. Van Foreest moves to eight points, while Abdusattorov has five. Caruana stretches his lead to four points Fabiano Caruana continued his unbeaten run by defeating Vincent Keymer with Black in their first game. Caruana gained the upper hand in the endgame and successfully converted his advantage. A draw in the return took Caruana to fourteen points from four wins and two draws, while Keymer finished the day on four. Le Quang Liem drew both games with Richard Rapport to reach ten points, four behind Caruana. Rapport moves to five. Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and Vladislav Artemiev also drew twice. Their first encounter lasted 89 moves. Artemiev has five points and Praggnanandhaa four. Martirosyan beats Carlsen to seize the Group C lead Haik Martirosyan produced the day’s standout result by inflicting Magnus Carlsen’s first Fast Classic defeat after four consecutive draws. Playing with White in the first game, Martirosyan launched a dangerous attack and eventually broke through to secure the victory. A draw in the return encounter gave Martirosyan four points from the pair and the outright Group C lead on ten. Carlsen has five. Shakhriyar Mamedyarov and Abhimanyu Mishra drew both encounters, taking them to seven and five points respectively. Anish Giri moved into second place on nine points after drawing his first game with Ian Nepomniachtchi and winning the return with White. Giri prevailed after a long battle, leaving Nepomniachtchi on seven. Shakhriyar Mamedyarov and Abhimanyu Mishra drew both encounters, taking them to seven and five points respectively. Vachier-Lagrave moves clear as Vaishali retaliates Maxime Vachier-Lagrave won the direct encounter between the Group D leaders. After drawing his first game with Hans Moke Niemann, he built up sustained pressure with White in the return and converted the advantage. Vachier-Lagrave reaches twelve points, three clear of Niemann. Arjun Erigaisi joined Niemann on nine points after a win and a draw against Wesley So. Erigaisi came under pressure in the first game but turned the tables to secure the victory. The return was drawn, leaving So on four. Bibisara Assaubayeva and Vaishali Rameshbabu exchanged wins with White. Assaubayeva struck first, but Vaishali responded with an attacking victory of her own to claim her first Fast Classic win of the event. Assaubayeva moves to eight points and Vaishali to four. The Fast Classic group stage continues on Saturday, November 14, with Games 7 and 8. Four games remain for each player before the group standings determine places in the six knockout brackets. Developed by Norway Chess and approved by FIDE, the Total Chess World Championship Tour introduces a unified format that crowns the world’s ultimate champion by testing excellence across three disciplines: Fast Classical, Rapid and Blitz. The Tour will bring together the world’s top 24 men and women players to compete across four premier international events hosted in leading global cities. Designed to elevate the sport’s commercial appeal and fan engagement, Total Chess combines world-class competition with innovation, technology and immersive spectator experiences to create a new benchmark for professional chess. With a vision to make chess one of the world’s most engaging and commercially sustainable sports, Total Chess aims to expand the game’s global footprint, inspire the next generation of players, and connect millions of fans through a dynamic championship that celebrates intelligence, strategy and sporting excellence.

title: Javokhir Sindarov is writing a new page in chess history
summary: From wunderkind to World Championship challenger, Javokhir Sindarov has enjoyed a remarkable succession of achievements. As he prepares for the greatest challenge of his young career, many experts regard him as the favourite to dethrone the equally young reigning champion. Javokhir Sindarov was born on 8 December 2005 in Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan. He learned the rules of chess at the age of four and soon claimed victory in the Asian School Chess Championship in the under-7 category. His rise continued at an extraordinary pace. He became an International Master in October 2017 and, just one year later, earned the title of Grandmaster. At the age of 12 years, 10 months and eight days, he became the second-youngest player in history at the time to achieve this distinction. In the summer of 2019, Sindarov captured the Uzbekistan national championship in emphatic fashion, scoring an impressive 10 points out of 12. He repeated the feat in 2021 and 2024, securing his second and third national titles. Photo: Frans Peters At the beginning of 2021, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev signed a decree aimed, among other objectives, at establishing Uzbekistan as one of the world’s leading chess nations. The country’s elite players benefited from this ambitious programme of support, and Sindarov eventually committed himself entirely to chess after a brief period of uncertainty about his future. His first major breakthrough on the international stage came at the 2021 World Cup in Sochi, Russia. There, he pulled off a stunning upset by eliminating tournament favourite Alireza Firouzja in the second round. Photo: Eric Rosen The following summer, Sindarov represented Uzbekistan on board three at the 2022 Chess Olympiad in Chennai. Scoring a solid 6½ points from ten games, he made a valuable contribution to his country’s sensational gold-medal triumph. Uzbekistan’s historic victory provided further evidence of the remarkable potential of its young generation and justified the government’s investment in chess development. Photo: Lennart Ootes Sindarov continued his steady ascent through the world rankings in 2023, producing strong performances at the World Cup in Baku and the Asian Games in Hangzhou. By the end of the year, he had crossed the coveted 2700-rating threshold, confirming his arrival among the world’s elite. After a period of relative stagnation, the defining breakthrough came in 2025. Following a series of impressive performances across several competitions, the almost 20-year-old produced a brilliant performance at the World Cup in Goa, claiming the title and securing his place in the Candidates Tournament. Photo: Michal Walusza Held in Cyprus in March and April 2026, the Candidates Tournament brought together eight of the world’s strongest players to determine the challenger for the World Championship. Sindarov made an extraordinary start, winning five of his first six games. He never relinquished his grip on the tournament, going on to dominate the competition in a manner unprecedented in the history of the modern eight-player, double-round-robin Candidates format. His triumph earned him the right to challenge reigning World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju at the end of 2026. Photo: Niki Riga Sindarov will therefore enter the Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 with considerable confidence. His recent achievements suggest that he is approaching the contest in excellent form. Most notably, he helped Uzbekistan secure its second Olympic gold medal at the Olympiad in Samarkand last September. Playing on board two, Sindarov scored seven points from ten games and also claimed the individual bronze medal. The key to the match will undoubtedly lie in Sindarov’s ability to exploit his principal strengths: an aggressive playing style, exceptional calculation speed and precision, and outstanding tactical acuity. Opening preparation will naturally play a crucial role, particularly as both contenders have demonstrated considerable sophistication and resourcefulness in this area. Both players have also shown impressive mental resilience in critical moments, as well as the ability to recover from occasional setbacks in high-pressure competitions. Such qualities could prove decisive in a match where the psychological battle may be every bit as important as the moves played on the board. Photo: Michal Walusza This encounter between two of the finest representatives of chess superpowers promises to be a fascinating clash of ambition, talent, and determination. Confidence will undoubtedly be a decisive factor. Sindarov appears to have the psychological advantage on the strength of his recent results, but the balance of power can shift remarkably quickly in a World Championship match. Much may depend on the outcome of the opening games and how each player responds to the inevitable pressure of the occasion. Ultimately, the question is an intriguing one: Will Sindarov’s hunger to claim the highest title outweigh Gukesh’s experience of having already conquered the summit of the chess world? Written by Yannick Pelletier The Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 is taking place at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, near Geneva, Switzerland, November 22 to December 12. The first round will be played on November 24. All information on the schedule can be found on the Championship website. Tickets to the playing hall and the fan zone can be bought on the designated website: https://tickets.fide.com/en , while games can be watched on the FIDE YouTube channel.

title: Six World Amateur Chess Champions crowned in Klang, Malaysia
summary: The FIDE World Amateur Chess Championships 2026 concluded at the KSL Esplanade Hotel with two titles decided on tiebreaks and Mongolia’s Javkhlan Bayarjargal posting the highest score of the event, 8½/9. Malaysia’s Aqil Ainuddin Naufal Akhramsyah Muammar Ubaidah won Open U2000 unbeaten with 8/9, while Indian, Kazakhstani, Mongolian and Ukrainian players claimed the other titles. Open U2300 – Tulegenov wins a three-way tie Kazakhstan’s Amir Tulegenov drew with Malaysia’s FM Genivan Genkeswaran in his final-round game to finish on 7/9. Vietnam’s CM Tran Pham Quang Minh and Poland’s CM Tomasz Jaskolka both won to match his score. Tulegenov took gold on tiebreak, ahead of Tran and Jaskolka. Jaskolka’s victory over overnight co-leader FM Nestor Favian Lozano Ramirez completely reshaped the podium in the final round. Women’s U2300 – Pavithra seals the title unbeaten India’s Pavithra R V drew her final-round game with Uzbekistan’s WCM Mumtozbegim Mansurova to preserve her half-point lead and finish unbeaten on 7½/9. Mansurova took silver with 7/9. Malaysia’s WCM Nithyalakshmi Sivanesan drew with Kazakhstan’s WCM Kristina Kim to secure bronze on 6/9. Open U2000 – Aqil wins gold for Malaysia Malaysia’s Aqil Ainuddin Naufal Akhramsyah Muammar Ubaidah drew with Kazakhstan’s Mukhtar Ainakul on the top board to finish a full point clear on 8/9, with seven wins and two draws. Ainakul took silver on tiebreak with 7/9, ahead of India’s C Maniswar, who earned bronze after defeating his compatriot Ashutosh Kumar. Women’s U2000 – Osadchuk finishes a point clear Ukraine’s Anastasiia Osadchuk secured the title in Round 8, finishing with 7½/9. Malaysia’s Nur Ain Shahar defeated the champion in the final round and placed fourth on 6/9. Mongolia’s WCM Odmaa Enkhsaikhan won her final game to claim silver on 6½/9, while her compatriot Naranzaya Zorigoo took bronze on tiebreak ahead of Shahar. Open U1700 – Javkhlan scores 8½/9 Mongolia’s Javkhlan Bayarjargal defeated India’s Anshu Kr Pathak in the final round to complete an unbeaten campaign with eight wins and one draw. China’s Tang Keran beat Mongolia’s Munkhbat Batnyam in the final round to take silver on 7½/9. Munkhbat earned bronze on tiebreak with 7/9. Women’s U1700 – Dolgormaa claims gold on tiebreak Mongolia’s Dolgormaa Lkhavgasuren and Sod-Erdene Naranbaatar both finished on 7½/9, with Dolgormaa taking gold on tiebreak. Malaysia’s Kuan Rhe Anne defeated Dolgormaa on the top board to earn bronze with 7/9, while Sod-Erdene beat Malaysia’s WCM Farah Liyana Salihin to draw level with the leader. title: Faster 60- and 45-minute time controls now eligible for ratings and norms, federations to review changes
summary: The FIDE Council has issued a Resolution allowing shorter time controls to be eligible for standard ratings and title norms. While the new regulations take effect immediately, the discussion is not over yet. National federations will review the changes ahead of an extraordinary General Assembly in December, where further amendments may be proposed. Time controls of 60 and 45 minutes per player have grown significantly in popularity in recent years. One of the early pioneers of faster classical formats at the elite level was organiser Oleg Skvortsov, whose Zurich Chess Challenge events helped popularise 40-minute games among top players in the mid-2010s. In response to growing demand from the chess community, in autumn of 2025 FIDE launched a pilot project to count these shorter time controls for classic rating. Discussions on recognising them for rating and norm purposes continued throughout 2025 and 2026. Following extensive feedback from players, organisers, partners, leading grandmasters, and discussion during the 2026 General Assembly, FIDE decided to update its regulations to better reflect the evolving needs of the chess world. Going forward, 60’+30” will be considered a standard time control. It will not require special approval, will be eligible for standard rating, and may be used for title norms. The shorter 45’+30” time control may now also be used in tournaments that are eligible for the FIDE Circuit, as well as in events where no player rated above 2400 participates. However, for these time controls to count towards standard ratings and title norms, two major restrictions apply: No more than two rounds may be held per day. However, if a tournament is rated only for rating purposes and no norms or titles can be earned, the rule is more flexible: the total playing time may not exceed 12 hours per day. As a result, such tournaments may hold more than two rounds per day. No more than one norm achieved in such events may be counted towards a single title. These restrictions are not necessarily permanent. The Qualification Commission has been tasked with studying the impact of the changes and submitting recommendations on whether the 45’+30” format should become a permanent standard time control and whether tournaments played with 45’+30” and 60’+30” should count towards titles and norms without restrictions. Although the Resolution is already in effect, consultations with national federations will continue. FIDE has distributed a briefing paper outlining the background, timeline and rationale behind the changes and has invited feedback from federations and leading players. An extraordinary General Assembly will be held in December to discuss the new regulations. Should federations propose amendments, the FIDE Council will follow with adjustments. “The world is changing rapidly, and chess is evolving with it. FIDE must adapt accordingly. These new regulations introduce changes long requested by players and organisers,” said FIDE President Timur Turlov. “At the same time, we have a responsibility to preserve the prestige of chess titles and ensure a smooth transition without creating unnecessary burdens for players, which is why certain restrictions remain in place. National federations will have the opportunity to discuss these changes in December, and if further adjustments are needed, we are ready to make them.” The full text of the Resolution is available HERE.

title: Review: Robert Ris' FritzTrainers on openings, calculation and strategic thinking (Part 3)
summary:
“The third and final part of my author special on Robert Ris rounds off my review of his work by looking at his middlegame courses, which focus primarily on chess strategy,” writes Lukas Köpl in his comprehensive review of Robert Ris’s video courses.

Part III • Strategic and Positional Play

Strategy is an important part of the development of chess players who have already learned the basics. At first, however, it can seem overwhelming, as players have to deal with concepts and individual aspects of pawn play and piece play that make up a chess position. Terms such as weak square, bad piece, space advantage or prophylaxis are quickly explained, but knowing their definitions is still a long way from being able to apply them in practice.

It is not enough simply to rely on rules of thumb. Instead, players need to develop sound mental images and an understanding of how individual strategic features can influence one another and affect the position as a whole.

Robert Ris addresses this problem by consistently linking positional features, plans and their concrete execution. His earlier course Strategy Training: How to Make a Plan and the three-part series Mastering Chess Strategy together form a course of instruction that ranges from basic strategic vocabulary to developing plans that take the opponent's intentions into account.

In doing so, Ris avoids two common extremes. He neither reduces strategy to rules of thumb nor dissolves it entirely into engine variations. Instead, he shows that a plan is derived from the features of a position. Which pawn can create a lever? Which tension should be maintained or resolved? Which piece is limiting the coordination of your forces? What target can be created? What does the opponent intend to do next? These questions lead from describing a position to making decisions.

Strategy Training: How to Make a Plan (2019)

How to Make a Plan aims to teach the methods by which a plan can be formulated for a given position. The idea is not to develop an all-encompassing master plan, but rather to provide guidance on how to formulate a plan, or a mini-plan, in any position, regardless of its complexity.

Ris reduces his method to five key aspects that players should make use of:

1. The influence of pawn play

2. Dealing with tension

3. Improving the worst-placed piece

4. Creating and exploiting weaknesses

5. Prophylactic thinking

These are certainly familiar questions that can also be found in the relevant literature on the subject. One could argue that a universal method of finding plans might require an even finer subdivision, but that perhaps depends more on the chess "school" in which one was brought up.

These five key ideas are discussed through illustrative games, which sometimes make it particularly clear how closely the five aspects are intertwined.

The game examples, however, are not merely presented as lectures. Rather, they provide the basis for the test positions that follow. There are plenty of these, allowing players to practise each of the five techniques extensively.

Basics of Chess Strategy Vol. 1 – Concepts of Pawn Play

Some time after this broad outline of how to find a plan, Ris followed up with a three-part series devoted to the study of strategic play, incorporating aspects from the course Chess Training – How to Make Plan . The individual elements that make up a position are examined in greater detail.

Basics of Chess Strategy Vol. 1 begins with the functions of pawns: king protection, support for the pieces, restriction of the opponent's mobility, weak pawns, weak squares and typical pawn structures. Open files and the seventh rank as the natural domain of the rooks are also covered. This breaks down the common distinction between "strategic" and "attacking" play. A rook on the seventh rank is positionally justified and at the same time poses tactical threats; a weak square is only relevant if a piece can occupy it and exert an influence from there.

The strength of the first volume lies in its concrete approach. Ris does not treat pawns as an isolated feature, but shows how they interact with the other aspects of piece play. An isolated or backward pawn is not automatically a weakness – what matters is whether it can be attacked, the activity of the pieces and the possibilities for dynamic counterplay.

For beginners, this is an important lesson in avoiding rigid rules and losing their sense of dynamics. For stronger players, the volume serves as a systematic review, especially if they make a serious effort to solve the numerous exercises. From a trainer's perspective, I can say that this took a great deal of time, but it also provided me with a useful collection of material to supplement my existing exercises on the individual topics.

Mastering Chess Strategy Vol. 2: Concepts of Piece Play

Mastering Chess Strategy Vol. 2 , published in 2025, shifts the focus to the handling of pieces. Which piece is well placed, which is badly placed, and what can be done to improve the situation? The central topics are improving the worst-placed piece, finding suitable squares, decisions about exchanges and coordination.

These topics are fundamental, but the way they interact is complex. A piece may be badly placed in principle and still perform an important defensive function. An exchange may create space but leave the opponent with a strong square. It is precisely this interaction that makes the series so appealing to me, because, compared with other approaches, it does not neglect dynamics and the resulting interplay of different factors.

Pieces are assessed according to the tasks they perform, the pawn levers they support and whether improving them makes a concrete plan possible. The course is particularly suitable for players who can describe positions correctly but then struggle to find a sequence of moves.

Mastering Chess Strategy Vol. 3:

Identifying, Prioritising and Attacking Weaknesses

Mastering Chess Strategy Vol. 3 concludes the trilogy by examining how to exploit the opponent's weaknesses. Weak pawns, a vulnerable king and poor piece coordination are not merely identified – the player must determine the most important target, prioritise the attack and develop a plan that can be carried out. This represents a decisive step beyond static positional evaluation. Many club players identify several weaknesses but attack the wrong one or switch targets before their pieces are ready.

As already mentioned in connection with the series, Ris's approach deserves particular emphasis here: strategy is not enough without tactical awareness. A weakness often becomes exploitable only through a concrete threat. Conversely, attacking a target may give the opponent a tactical resource. Volume 3 thus leads back to the series on calculation, creating a valuable connection between the two.

It is precisely this relationship between the different areas that makes the complete work stronger: understand the position, choose a plan, calculate the variations. This brings everything together into a well-structured course of instruction on the middlegame.

Conclusion

For players rated below 1600, Volume 1 is the natural starting point, followed by selected chapters from How to Make a Plan . Between 1600 and 2000, the complete trilogy is recommended, with each unit supplemented by examples from the player's own games. Above 2000, the value lies less in learning new concepts than in systematising existing knowledge and working through the exercises. At this level, How to Make a Plan is often the more compact standalone course. For trainers, the package is particularly attractive because it offers a clear progression from positional features through piece play to the selection of targets.

***

About the author:

International Master Robert Ris (born in 1988) has successfully represented his home country, the Netherlands, at numerous youth championships. Today, he is primarily active as a chess trainer in schools and chess clubs and coaches students from various countries online at playchess.com. He has also worked as a live commentator for the Dutch Championship and the traditional tournament in Wijk aan Zee.

The Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot takes place from 10 to 20 November at the Anantara New York Palace Hotel in Budapest. Developed by Norway Chess and approved by FIDE, the competition combines three different time controls. The event serves as a test for the Total Chess World Championship Tour, which is scheduled to begin in 2027.

The 24 participants include Magnus Carlsen, Fabiano Caruana, Vincent Keymer, Wesley So, Anish Giri, Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Hungary's Richard Rapport.

The tournament consists of three stages:

Blitz tournament (10 November): The event begins with all 24 participants playing nine rounds of blitz chess (3+2) under the Swiss system. The final standings will later serve as a tiebreak and influence the pairings in the knockout stage. Magnus Carlsen won ahead of Maxime Vachier-Lagrave and Levon Aronian.

Group stage (11–15 November): The players are divided into four groups of six. Within each group, everyone plays everyone else twice, once with White and once with Black. The time control is 45 minutes plus 30 seconds per move. A win earns three points and a draw one point. The games are rated and count towards the FIDE rating list.

Knockout stage (17–20 November): After a rest day, the players are divided into six separate knockout competitions according to their group-stage standings. Only the four group winners compete for the overall tournament victory. Each knockout match lasts two days. On each day, the players contest four blitz games, two rapid games (15+10) and one game with 45 minutes plus 30 seconds per move. Games played at longer time controls carry more weight than blitz games. If the match remains tied after the two days, an Armageddon game decides the winner.
